passage:
I'm Rohan. Last week Elizabeth's mock results came back and she told everyone at school her life was over, flat, like a fact. On Sunday I went to her house to return a book and found her on the verandah with her grandfather Francis, who was peeling a mango.
I stayed quiet by the gate. Francis told her that at nineteen he had been sacked from a printing press and walked home twelve kilometres with his tools in a sack. "I thought that was the end of me. Then a man at the corner shop needed a hand with his accounts." He kept peeling as he talked.
Elizabeth didn't say anything, but she stopped hugging her knees. I can't tell what she really thought. On Monday, though, she stopped saying "over" and asked me to share my notes.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth's grandfather Francis do at the printing press at nineteen?
qa.a: He was sacked from it and walked home twelve kilometres with his tools in a sack.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling before Francis told his story?
qa.a: She was in despair and very worried about the mock results, since she declared her life was over. Her hugged knees suggest she felt small and stuck.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do next to use what she heard from Francis?
qa.a: She could ask him what he did in the weeks after and then plan one small step for her own exams, such as going through her notes with a friend.

qa.q: How might Francis have felt telling Elizabeth about being sacked?
qa.a: He may have felt a little vulnerable, but calm and caring. He kept peeling the mango and told it plainly, without a lecture, as a way to be near her.

grounding: A grandparent's story of a hard time gives a teenager a longer view of her own trouble, seen by an onlooker.

passage:
Friday. Bhavna was rejected from the school debate team and threw her bag on the bed without a word. Even her favourite dal at dinner went untouched. "I'm just not good at anything," she muttered.
Saturday evening. Her grandfather Chinmay knocked on her door. "Walk with me to the park?" On the path he told her about the year the rains failed and he left his village at seventeen to work at a cement plant. "I hated it. I cried in the bunk at night. Six years later I was managing that plant, and I still didn't feel sure of myself." He never told her what to do.
The next Thursday, Bhavna signed up for the debate club's practice session as an audience member. "Just to watch," she told him. He nodded, and asked nothing else.

qa.q: Which team rejected Bhavna?
qa.a: The school debate team rejected her.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling after the rejection?
qa.a: She was hurt and discouraged. She left her favourite dal untouched and said she was not good at anything.

qa.q: What did Bhavna choose to do the following Thursday?
qa.a: She signed up to watch the debate club's practice as an audience member. It was a small step that kept the door open without demanding a big decision.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have shared his story instead of giving advice?
qa.a: His own hard years show that a setback can be long but is not the end. Telling it beside her gave Bhavna a longer timeline for her trouble without telling her what to do.

grounding: A grandparent's account of hardship and choices lengthens a teenager's view of her own setback.

passage: The power went at eight, right in the middle of exam week. Vijay sat on the stairs with the phone torch, his mock-test paper crumpled in his fist. Thirty-one out of a hundred. "My life is finished," he muttered. Sharmila, his older sister, rolled her eyes, but Dadi called them both to the veranda where the candle was burning. She didn't give advice. She told them about the year she was fifteen, when her father's shop burned down and she had to leave school for two years to help. "I cried every night. Then I went back, finished, became a teacher. Thirty-eight years I taught." She laughed softly. "The fire felt like the end. It was one bad chapter." Vijay smoothed the paper on his knee. The power came back an hour later, but he stayed on the veranda.

qa.q: What score did Vijay get on his mock test?
qa.a: Thirty-one out of a hundred.

qa.q: How can you tell Dadi's story changed how Vijay felt?
qa.a: He went from muttering that his life was finished to smoothing the paper on his knee and staying on the veranda, which suggests he felt calmer and less hopeless.

qa.q: What small step could help Vijay after the veranda talk?
qa.a: He could look at which questions he got wrong with his teacher or Sharmila and plan the next week's revision, treating the test as one chapter.

qa.q: Why might Dadi have told a story instead of giving advice?
qa.a: Her own years of loss and return let Vijay feel a longer timeline himself, which a lecture about marks probably could not have done.

grounding: Shows a grandmother's story of hardship giving a teenager a longer view of his own setback, more than advice could.

passage: Bhavna lost the school council election by nine votes, and the list was pinned up by lunchtime. By evening she had deleted her campaign posts and refused to come out for dinner. Her cousin Pankaj knocked, then gave up. It was Nana who came in with two cups of warm milk and sat on the edge of her bed. He told her about the union vote at the textile mill, back when he was twenty. He had lost to a man who later became his closest friend at the mill. "I was so angry I didn't talk to him for a month," Nana said. "Then his wife fell ill and I covered his shifts. Fifty years later, that loss is the least important thing I remember." Bhavna said nothing. But the next morning, she congratulated the winner at the gate.

qa.q: By how many votes did Bhavna lose the election?
qa.a: She lost by nine votes.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling on the evening of the loss?
qa.a: She was hurt and humiliated, deleting her campaign posts and refusing to come out for dinner.

qa.q: Why did Nana's story reach Bhavna when her cousin's knock did not?
qa.a: Nana sat with her and shared a real memory of losing, instead of lecturing, which let Bhavna draw her own lesson.

qa.q: How might the winner have seen Bhavna's congratulations at the gate?
qa.a: The winner was probably surprised and relieved to be greeted warmly, rather than facing a grudge from the girl who lost.

grounding: Shows a grandfather's story of an old loss giving a teenager a longer timeline for her own disappointment.

passage:
"You're not eating, Kiran," Ajji said, tapping the steel plate.
"Not hungry. They cut me from the state team. After two years of training."
Chinmay, eight, looked up from his rice. "Does that mean you're bad at hockey?"
"Chinmay!" Ajji hushed him, then turned back. "Kiran, did I ever tell you about my singing?"
"You sing?"
"Once. I wanted to sing on the radio. I failed the audition three times. The third time I came home and cut all my hair short out of anger." Ajji laughed. "My mother cried more about the hair."
"And then?"
"And then I sang for the temple, for weddings, for your father when he couldn't sleep. Fifty years, kanna. Never on the radio. Still, singing gave me my whole life."
Kiran was quiet. Then: "Okay. Pass the rasam."

qa.q: How many times did Ajji fail the radio audition?
qa.a: She failed it three times.

qa.q: What does Kiran asking for rasam suggest about how Kiran felt after the story?
qa.a: It suggests Kiran felt a little lighter and less crushed, ready to eat again after hearing that Ajji's failure did not end her singing.

qa.q: How could an elder help a teenager after a big disappointment?
qa.a: Like Ajji, they could share a true story of their own setback and what came after, instead of telling the teen how to feel.

qa.q: What is it like for Chinmay to watch this conversation?
qa.a: Chinmay is young and blunt, and probably learns from the story too, seeing that a failure is not the same as being bad at something.

grounding: Shows a teenager receiving a grandmother's story of failure that gives a longer perspective on being cut from a team.

passage: Last winter, when my name was missing from the district basketball list, I decided my life was basically finished. I'm Rukmini, and I was very dramatic about it. Everyone gave advice. "Try next year." "Focus on studies." I stopped hearing any of it. Then one night Gopika Paati, who never talks about the past, sat on the edge of my bed and told me about the year she turned nineteen. The mill closed, and she lost the only job in the family. She cried for a week, then learned typing on a borrowed machine, and two years later she was the fastest typist at the collector's office. "That week felt like forever," she said. "Now it's one line in a long story." She didn't tell me what to do. But I started counting my life in decades instead of weeks. I made the list this October.

qa.q: What did Gopika Paati learn after she lost her mill job?
qa.a: She learned typing on a borrowed machine.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel when the name was missing from the list?
qa.a: Rukmini felt crushed and hopeless, deciding life was basically finished and no longer hearing anyone's advice.

qa.q: Why did Paati's story help more than the advice?
qa.a: It showed a real hard week inside a long life, so Rukmini could feel the longer timeline instead of just being told to wait.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Gopika Paati to share that memory?
qa.a: Since she never talks about the past, it may have felt tender to reopen, and also warm to see her hard week help Rukmini.

grounding: Shows a grandparent's story of hardship and recovery giving a teenager a longer timeline for a sports setback than advice alone could.
